title: Kara: the steel circle
hook: a steel bracelet, a circle without end, reminding the hand what it's for

segments.voice: Yesterday, kangha, the small comb. Your line was clean and ordered. Did you tidy one thing, gently? Today, the K you've most likely already seen, on a wrist at the next desk. Day two hundred sixty-seven.

Some people tie a string around a finger so they won't forget something. Others write a word on the back of their hand. The trick works because hands are always in front of us: typing, reaching, holding a cup, holding a phone. If you want a reminder you'll see a hundred times a day, put it on your hand. Sikhs have been doing this for centuries, with a plain circle of steel at the wrist. You've probably seen one. Today, the third of the five Ks: kara.
screen: `A STRING ON A FINGER.` → `HANDS, ALWAYS IN VIEW.` → `A STEEL CIRCLE AT THE WRIST.`

segments.voice: Kara means a bracelet, and the Sikh kara is a very particular one: plain steel or iron, no gold, no gems, no decoration. Most Sikhs wear it on the wrist of the hand they use most, often the right. And it carries three ideas, each simple. First, the circle. It has no beginning and no end, and Sikhs often say that's a picture of God, the One without beginning or end, and of the unbroken bond between a Sikh and the Guru. Second, the steel. Not gold, which says wealth, or silver, which says status. Steel is what tools and plows are made of, humble and strong. Rich or poor, a Sikh wears the same kara. Third, and this is the one people remember: the hand. Every time the hand moves, the kara moves with it. Reaching for something that isn't yours, raising a fist in anger, signing a dishonest paper: the steel is right there, catching the light, asking a quiet question. What are these hands doing? It's the same question under the whole rehat. The Gurus taught kirat karni, honest work with your own hands, and seva, service with your own hands. The kara just keeps the question on your wrist. It's also the most widely worn of the five Ks. Many Sikhs who don't keep all five still wear a kara, and you'll see them on Punjabi wrists of many backgrounds. Plain, heavy, cool against the skin, and never quite letting you forget.
screen: `KARA — PLAIN STEEL, NO GOLD.` · `A CIRCLE: NO BEGINNING, NO END.` · `STEEL: HUMBLE, STRONG, THE SAME FOR ALL.` · `ON THE HAND THAT ACTS.` · then, large: `WHAT ARE THESE HANDS DOING.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up. Look at them. Think of what they've done today: what they carried, typed, cooked, held, maybe what they shouldn't have done. No scolding; just honest looking. Then choose one good thing these hands will do before the day ends. Picture it. Let the hands rest, open, while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Kara. The plain steel bracelet, the third K: a circle without end, the same for rich and poor, reminding the hand what it's for.
Your line: what are these hands doing. Today, whenever you notice your wrist, ask the question once, and do the one good thing you chose. Day two hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the five Ks wear a plain steel or iron kara on the wrist, and many other Sikhs wear one too, as a constant reminder of the Guru and of what their hands should do.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kara, the steel bracelet; the ੜ is a flapped r, made with a quick flick of the tongue.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Sikh bracelet.
what it means: a plain steel circle on the hand that acts: God without end, the bond with the Guru, and a question about what the hand is doing.
what a scholar hears: sarab loh, all-steel or iron, is preferred to precious metal; the kara is the third of the five Ks and the one most often worn by Sikhs who aren't amritdhari.
